attributes.readMe:
## Automation

Runs a Realm Runner script with nobody watching: on a schedule, once at a set time, or when another service sends a webhook. The card says which script runs, when, which outside services the script may call, and what each run and each month may use.

![The isolated view: state, payer, next and last run, the script and each trigger in words](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cardstack/boxel-catalog/6a4c47249a75abb63ec7539b88febde36bc9a34f/automation/Spec/images/isolated.png)

```ts
import { Automation } from '@cardstack/catalog/automation/automation';
@field automation = linksTo(Automation);
```

Create an Automation in the workspace the script works on, link the script, then add the triggers, outside services and limits. A type that extends `Automation` is an automation too.

### Who turns it on, and who pays

* A new automation runs nothing. Someone who can edit the workspace turns the automation on, and that person pays for every run. Each run acts as that person, within the card's limits.
* Editing the card never changes who pays. Raising a limit, or turning on batched AI, pauses the automation until someone turns the automation on again.
* Only people who can edit the workspace can change an automation. Sharing rules that let others edit some cards never reach an automation.

### What the card holds

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `script` | A JavaScript file in the same workspace, run as a Realm Runner script: the body of an async function with the `realm` object. The edit view edits and saves the file in place. |
| `triggers` | **Schedule**: a cron expression (or a macro such as `@daily`) in a time zone, at most once every 5 minutes, with an optional stop after a number of runs or after a date. **Once**: a date and a time in a time zone. **Webhook**: one of the workspace's incoming webhooks. Each trigger has a label, unique within the automation, that keeps the trigger's count of runs. |
| `operations` | The only outside calls the script may make: a card type and one of the type's `callApi` operations. |
| `caps` | For each run: outside calls, data received, saves, AI requests, AI spending in credits and run time (up to 20 minutes). For each day and each month: the credits all runs together may spend. A run stops at the first limit the run reaches. |
| `params` | Values the script reads as `realm.current.automation.params`. |
| `batchedAI`, `batchDeadlineMinutes` | AI requests at about half the price, answered later. The deadline is how long a run waits for the answers, up to 1,440 minutes and an hour when empty; Boxel asks again at full price for any answer not back by then. |

Whether an automation is on, who pays, the next run and the run counts live on the server, not on the card.

### Run milestones

A script names its milestones up front, then marks each one as the script reaches it. The card reads the milestones from the runs, never from a field.

```js
realm.progress.plan(['Fetch open issues', 'Group by label', 'Write digest']);
realm.progress.milestone('Fetch open issues');
// …
realm.progress.count(done, issues.length);
realm.progress.milestone('Group by label');
```

* `realm.progress.plan([...names])` declares 1 to 50 names, in order. Write the plan as a list of names: the card reads the plan from the script's text to show the milestones ahead before any run.
* `realm.progress.milestone(name)` starts that milestone and ends the one before. A name the plan doesn't list still counts, and shows as not in the plan.
* `realm.progress.count(done, total)` says how far the script is through the current milestone. Count in steps, such as every hundredth item: a run records at most 200 milestones and 5,000 progress and console calls.
* None of the three needs `await`. A bad argument throws in the script.

### What each format shows

Only people who can edit the workspace see the state, the payer, the runs and a run's milestones. The card names the payer only to an editor who shares a workspace with the payer. Anyone else, and a prerendered view, sees the card's own fields and the milestones the script declares.

* **Isolated**: everything on the card, with the state and the reason for a pause, the payer, the next and last run, each trigger's runs and runs left, and each milestone of the run in progress or the last run, with its time and count.
* **Embedded**: the title and state, every trigger in words, the next and last run, and the milestones. A narrow row shows the milestones as a bar under where the run stands, such as *Failed in Match invoices*. A row 36rem wide or more shows each milestone on a track with its time, for runs of up to 8 milestones.

![The embedded view of a run in progress, with each milestone on a track](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cardstack/boxel-catalog/6a4c47249a75abb63ec7539b88febde36bc9a34f/automation/Spec/images/embedded.png)

* **Fitted**: each size adds the next most useful fact. A badge or strip shows the title and, from 240px wide, the state. Then the first trigger, or where a running or failed run stands. Then the milestones as a bar. A tile adds the next and last run and any warning (*No script yet*, *Batched AI*). A tall tile or a card lists the milestones around the current one.

![The fitted view as a strip, a tile, a large tile and a card](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cardstack/boxel-catalog/6a4c47249a75abb63ec7539b88febde36bc9a34f/automation/Spec/images/fitted.png)

### The linked examples

Neither example is turned on.

* `Automation/weekly-card-count` counts the workspace's cards by type every Monday at 7:00 AM Chicago time, and whenever its webhook is called, into `reports/card-count.md`. A search answers 50 cards a page unless `page.size` asks for up to 100, so the script reads 100 cards at a time, asking for the next `page.number` until `truncated` is false. Two milestones, the first with a count.
* `Automation/open-issues-digest` reads the open issues of the GitHub repository card `examples/GitHubRepository/boxel` every weekday morning, twice a day on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and once at a kick-off, and groups them by label into `reports/open-issues.md`. Its one outside call is the repository type's `openIssues`, made with the GitHub key of whoever turns the automation on. Three milestones.

### Non-goals

* **Not a way to run any code.** An automation runs a Realm Runner script, never a card's command or a module the card names.
* **Not a way around the workspace's permissions.** A run acts as the person who turned the automation on, reaches outside the workspace only through its declared outside calls and AI requests, and its saves land together when the run finishes, or not at all.
